sentences.text: Thecodontosaurus was a small, two-legged creature measuring about two meters in total length, though average specimens were shorter at 1.2 meters long.
Its name means "socket-tooth" because the teeth sat in separate sockets rather than being fused to the jaw bone.
The animal possessed a narrow skull with many small to medium-sized, leaf-shaped, serrated teeth that were curved.
It had five digits on its hands and feet, featuring long, narrow hands with an extended claw on each.
The largest known individuals of Thecodontosaurus reached an estimated length of 2.5 meters.
Muscle attachment studies suggest Thecodontosaurus was an extremely fast bipedal runner that used its weaker front limbs to grasp and process vegetation.
John Morris provided the complete species name Thecodontosaurus antiquus in 1843.
Thomas Huxley was the first to recognize Thecodontosaurus as a dinosaur in 1870, though he incorrectly placed it in the Scelidosauridae.
The parent group of the genus Thecodontosaurus is Sauropodomorpha.
Remains of Thecodontosaurus are primarily found in Triassic fissure fillings in southern England.
In 2000, Michael Benton suggested that a robust morph found in the population might represent either a second species or sexual dimorphism.
The hypothesis that carnivorous prosauropods with the body of Thecodontosaurus and slicing teeth existed has been totally discredited, although defended by Michael Cooper in 1981.
In 2020, Ballell, Rayfield, and Benton suggested that Pantydraco caducus might be a taxon of uncertain validity or a juvenile of Thecodontosaurus antiquus.
